docs.title: ThingLarp IoT Platform
docs.text:
ThingLarp is a high-performance, completely unconstrained IoT telemetry and analytics platform built as an open, modern alternative to ThingSpeak.

It provides native MQTT ingestion, dynamic field auto-discovery without prior schema definitions, microsecond time-series storage powered by TimescaleDB, and an cross-platform Flutter dashboard for desktop, mobile, and web.

⚡ Vibe Coding Disclaimer

This project was mostly vibe coded by Antigravity (Google DeepMind's agentic AI assistant) in close collaboration with @iimarky123. While designed with production-grade architectural patterns, microservices, and end-to-end verification tests, please review all configurations and security secrets before deploying to critical production infrastructure.

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
🚀 No Rate Limits📈 Unlimited Dynamic Fields🔒 Strict Multi-Tenant Security⚡ TimescaleDB Continuous Aggregates📱 Cross-Platform Flutter Dashboard

Unlike legacy IoT platforms that throttle free tiers to 1 update every 15–60 seconds, ThingLarp enforces zero artificial rate limits. High-frequency sensors (vibration, acoustics, motor RPM) can stream at 50Hz–100Hz continuously.

No more restriction to 8 numeric fields (field1...field8). Devices can publish arbitrary JSON key-value pairs (e.g. {"temp": 24.5, "co2_ppm": 420, "gyro_z": -0.012}). Fields are dynamically discovered, indexed, and charted on the fly.

Every MQTT publish and subscribe is strictly authorized at the broker level using mosquitto-go-auth and PostgreSQL views. Devices can only publish to their provisioned channel; client apps can only subscribe to channels they own or are public.

Raw sensor readings are ingested into compressed hypertables with background continuous aggregate views (points_1m and points_1h). Queries across months of data return in milliseconds.

A native Flutter client for Linux Desktop, macOS, Windows, Android, iOS, and Web featuring real-time MQTT streaming, dynamic metric cards, and responsive time-series charts powered by fl_chart.

docs.title: Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Component Description Edge Proxy Traefik v3 Reverse proxy terminating TLS, automated Let's Encrypt certificates, TCP/HTTP routing. MQTT Broker Eclipse Mosquitto High-concurrency MQTT broker with mosquitto-go-auth plugin validating credentials via Postgres. Ingestion Engine Python Bridge High-throughput asynchronous daemon using aiomqtt, orjson, and PostgreSQL COPY batching. Database TimescaleDB PostgreSQL 16 engine with automated chunk compression and 1-minute / 1-hour continuous rollups. REST API FastAPI Asynchronous REST gateway for user authentication (JWT/Argon2id), channel management, and telemetry queries. Client App Flutter 3.x Cross-platform frontend with reactive state management (provider) and interactive charting (fl_chart).

docs.title: Database Architecture & TimescaleDB Optimization
docs.text: The database is built on PostgreSQL 16 with the TimescaleDB extension. It uses a strict three-schema separation to enforce least-privilege security boundaries and optimal disk-space efficiency.

docs.title: Schema Separation
docs.text:
Database: iot
├── app                  # Relational Control Plane (Metadata, Users, Channels)
├── telemetry            # Time-Series Engine (Hypertables, Continuous Aggregates)
└── mqtt                 # Broker Authentication (Views & ACL Functions for Mosquitto)

docs.title: 1. app Schema (Relational Control Plane)
docs.text:
Stores all application state and relational metadata:

  • app.users: Registered users with Argon2id-hashed passwords.
  • app.channels: Telemetry channels created by users. Supports public or private visibility.
  • app.devices: Physical IoT hardware credentials (d_<random> username with Bcrypt-hashed password).
  • app.mqtt_sessions: Short-lived (24-hour) frontend MQTT credentials (s_<random> username with Bcrypt password).
  • app.api_keys: HTTP Ingestion/Export API keys (X-API-Key) stored as SHA-256 hashes with 'write' or 'read' scopes.
  • app.channel_fields: Dynamically discovered field catalog per channel (maps field names like "temperature" to numeric field_id).

docs.title: 2. telemetry Schema (Time-Series Engine)
docs.text:
Stores high-frequency sensor readings as TimescaleDB Hypertables:

  • telemetry.points: Narrow time-series table storing numeric metric points: 
    CREATE TABLE telemetry.points (
    time        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    channel_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    field_id    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    value       DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL
);
SELECT create_hypertable('telemetry.points', 'time', chunk_time_interval => INTERVAL '1 day');
  • telemetry.messages: Audit table storing complete raw JSON payloads and metadata: 
    CREATE TABLE telemetry.messages (
    time        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    channel_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    device_id   INTEGER,
    payload     JSONB NOT NULL
);
SELECT create_hypertable('telemetry.messages', 'time', chunk_time_interval => INTERVAL '1 day');

docs.title: 3. mqtt Schema (Broker Auth & ACL Views)
docs.text:
Segregated views consumed directly by mosquitto-go-auth:

  • mqtt.users_view: Returns (username, password_hash) by uniting active hardware devices, valid unexpired frontend sessions, and internal service accounts (svc_bridge, svc_api).
  • mqtt.acl_topics(username, acc): Stored function evaluated by the broker for every topic request:
  • acc = 1 (Read): Can subscribe or read if channel is owned by user or is public.
  • acc = 2 (Write): Can publish if username is the authorized device assigned to that channel or an internal service account.
  • acc = 4 (Subscribe): Same logic as Read.

docs.title: TimescaleDB Compression Policies
docs.text:
To minimize NVMe/SSD storage costs, TimescaleDB natively compresses chunks older than 3 days using columnar compression:

ALTER TABLE telemetry.points SET (
    timescaledb.compress,
    timescaledb.compress_segmentby = 'channel_id, field_id',
    timescaledb.compress_orderby = 'time DESC'
);

SELECT add_compression_policy('telemetry.points', INTERVAL '3 days');
  • Compression Ratio: Typical telemetry data achieves 90% to 95% compression (10x–20x disk reduction).
  • Segmenting: By grouping identical channel_id and field_id sequences together, compression achieves maximum delta-of-delta bit-packing.

docs.title: Continuous Aggregates (Downsampling)
docs.text: To ensure instantaneous chart loading across millions of data points, TimescaleDB maintains background materialized rollups:

docs.title: 1-Minute Rollups (telemetry.points_1m)
docs.text:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW telemetry.points_1m
WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS
SELECT 
    time_bucket('1 minute', time) AS bucket,
    channel_id,
    field_id,
    AVG(value) AS avg_value,
    MIN(value) AS min_value,
    MAX(value) AS max_value,
    COUNT(*) AS count
FROM telemetry.points
GROUP BY bucket, channel_id, field_id
WITH NO DATA;

SELECT add_continuous_aggregate_policy('telemetry.points_1m',
    start_offset => INTERVAL '1 day',
    end_offset => INTERVAL '1 minute',
    schedule_interval => INTERVAL '1 minute');

docs.title: 1-Hour Rollups (telemetry.points_1h)
docs.text:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW telemetry.points_1h
WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS
SELECT 
    time_bucket('1 hour', bucket) AS bucket,
    channel_id,
    field_id,
    AVG(avg_value) AS avg_value,
    MIN(min_value) AS min_value,
    MAX(max_value) AS max_value,
    SUM(count) AS count
FROM telemetry.points_1m
GROUP BY time_bucket('1 hour', bucket), channel_id, field_id
WITH NO DATA;

SELECT add_continuous_aggregate_policy('telemetry.points_1h',
    start_offset => INTERVAL '7 days',
    end_offset => INTERVAL '1 hour',
    schedule_interval => INTERVAL '1 hour');

docs.title: Least-Privilege Database Roles
docs.text: PostgreSQL Role Access Scope iot_mqtt_auth Read-only access to mqtt.users_view and execute access to mqtt.acl_topics(). Has zero access to app.* or telemetry.*. iot_bridge Read access to app.channel_fields, write access to app.channel_fields (for auto-discovery), and append (INSERT/COPY) access to telemetry.points and telemetry.messages. iot_api Full CRUD on app.*, SELECT on telemetry.* (including rollups), and INSERT on telemetry.* for HTTP write fallback.

docs.title: System Architecture & Ingestion Pipeline
docs.text: ThingLarp is designed as a decoupled, asynchronous microservices architecture that separates the high-frequency telemetry ingestion path from the relational metadata and analytical query path.

docs.title: Architectural Principles
docs.text:
1. Decoupled Ingestion Pipeline: Devices publish telemetry to MQTT topics (channels/{id}/data). Neither the API nor the device communicates directly with the database. The Python Ingestion Bridge acts as a dedicated worker group consuming via shared MQTT subscriptions.
  2. Strict Least-Privilege Authorization: Database access is segregated across dedicated PostgreSQL roles (iot_mqtt_auth, iot_bridge, iot_api) preventing any service from reading or mutating tables outside its operational scope.
  3. Optimized Time-Series Storage: Raw sensor readings are normalized into narrow rows (time, channel_id, field_id, value) within TimescaleDB hypertables, combined with chunk compression and background continuous aggregate materialization.
  4. Dual-Ingress Parity: HTTP REST writes (POST /channels/{id}/data) forward the payload directly to the internal MQTT broker. Live subscribers (such as Flutter dashboards) observe real-time events identically whether the source is MQTT or HTTP.

docs.title: End-to-End Ingestion Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Sensor as IoT Hardware (ESP32)
    participant Edge as Traefik v3 (:8883)
    participant Broker as Mosquitto Broker
    participant Auth as Mosquitto-go-auth
    participant DB as TimescaleDB
    participant Bridge as Python Bridge
    actor Client as Flutter App

    Note over Sensor,Broker: 1. Connection & Authorization
    Sensor->>Edge: Connect TLS (Username / Bcrypt Password)
    Edge->>Broker: Forward TCP :1883
    Broker->>Auth: Check credentials ($1, $2)
    Auth->>DB: Query mqtt.users_view
    DB-->>Auth: Password Hash (Bcrypt)
    Auth-->>Broker: Authenticated OK

    Note over Client,Broker: 2. Real-Time Dashboard Subscription
    Client->>Broker: Subscribe channels/42/data
    Broker->>Auth: Check ACL (Topic, Flag=4)
    Auth->>DB: Query mqtt.acl_topics(user, flag)
    DB-->>Auth: Authorized topics
    Broker-->>Client: Subscribed OK

    Note over Sensor,DB: 3. Telemetry Ingestion
    Sensor->>Broker: PUBLISH channels/42/data {"temp": 24.5, "co2": 420}
    Broker->>Client: Deliver Live Message
    Broker->>Bridge: Deliver via $share/ingest/channels/+/data
    Note over Bridge: Fast JSON parse (orjson)<br/>Extract numeric points<br/>Resolve/Cache field IDs
    Bridge->>DB: Batch COPY into telemetry.points & telemetry.messages
    Note over DB: Background TimescaleDB Engine:<br/>- Compress chunks older than 7d<br/>- Refresh continuous rollups (1m / 1h)

docs.title: 1. Edge Proxy (Traefik v3)
docs.text:
• Handles inbound network traffic from public networks.
  • Manages automatic Let's Encrypt TLS termination for both HTTP (:80, :443) and secure MQTT (:8883).
  • Provides reverse proxying to the internal Docker bridge network (edge and backend).

docs.title: 2. MQTT Broker (Eclipse Mosquitto + mosquitto-go-auth)
docs.text:
• Handles persistent connections from thousands of IoT devices and Flutter applications.
  • Dynamically queries PostgreSQL views for authentication and topic authorization checks on every connect, publish, and subscribe attempt.
  • Supports MQTT over WebSockets (:9001) for Flutter Web.

docs.title: 3. Ingestion Bridge (bridge/)
docs.text:
• Pure asynchronous Python daemon (aiomqtt + asyncpg).
  • Connects using shared subscriptions: $share/ingest/channels/+/data, allowing horizontal scaling across multiple container replicas without message duplication.
  • Micro-batches incoming messages and writes in bulk to TimescaleDB using PostgreSQL binary COPY protocol.

docs.title: 4. REST & Metadata API (api/)
docs.text:
• High-performance FastAPI application.
  • Exposes user registration, JWT generation, channel provisioning, device token generation, and API key management.
  • Provides optimized telemetry querying with automatic resolution downsampling (auto, 1m, 1h, raw).

docs.title: 5. Time-Series Database (TimescaleDB / PostgreSQL 16)
docs.text:
• Stores platform relational metadata (app schema), time-series hypertables (telemetry schema), and broker auth views (mqtt schema).
  • Automatically rolls up raw points into 1-minute and 1-hour pre-computed continuous aggregate views.

docs.title: Flutter Client Application
docs.text: The ThingLarp App (app/) is a cross-platform client developed with Flutter 3.x that runs on Linux Desktop, macOS, Windows, Android, iOS, and Web.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Dynamic Endpoints: Configure custom API endpoints and MQTT broker addresses on the fly with persistent local storage (SharedPreferences).
  • Interactive Time-Series Visualizations: Line charts powered by fl_chart with touch tooltips, dynamic multi-field coloring, and time-axis formatting.
  • Multi-Type Dashboard Widgets: Customize each field's visualization on the fly between Line Chart (time-series curve), Radial Gauge (270° gradient arc with min/max bounds), KPI Metric Card (bold hero readout with min/avg/max stats), and Status / LED Indicator (glowing active/inactive status beacon). Selections persist in TimescaleDB.
  • Dynamic Field Auto-Discovery: Badges and metric cards dynamically spawn as incoming JSON packets reveal new keys.
  • Real-Time MQTT Streaming: Direct subscription to live channel topics (channels/{id}/data) using ephemeral session tokens.
  • Resolution Selector: Toggle between Auto, Raw, 1-Minute, and 1-Hour historical aggregations.
  • Hardware & Device Access Control: Provision hardware credentials with granular permission scopes (Publish Only, Subscribe Only, or Full Pub/Sub) and an instant Active/Suspended toggle.
  • Downlink Remote Control & Commands: Send downstream actuator commands and control JSON packets to subscribed IoT nodes (channels/{id}/commands) with quick action presets (Relay ON/OFF, Reboot, LED Toggle).
  • Data Export & Download: Export telemetry directly to CSV spreadsheets or JSON arrays with customizable time windows and resolution aggregations.
  • Data Import & Migration Tool: Import historical data from ThingSpeak CSV files or standard CSV formats with automatic column and field discovery.
  • Data Purge / Clear: Safely clear historical telemetry and message logs with confirmation safeguards while keeping field schemas intact.

docs.title: 2. Authentication & Data Service (iot_api_service.dart)
docs.text:
import 'dart:convert';
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

class IotApiService {
  final String baseUrl;
  String? _jwtToken;

  IotApiService({required this.baseUrl});

  // 1. User Login
  Future<bool> login(String username, String password) async {
    final response = await http.post(
      Uri.parse('$baseUrl/auth/login'),
      headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'},
      body: jsonEncode({'username': username, 'password': password}),
    );

    if (response.statusCode == 200) {
      final data = jsonDecode(response.body);
      _jwtToken = data['access_token'];
      return true;
    }
    return false;
  }

  // 2. Request Short-Lived MQTT Session Token
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> requestMqttSession() async {
    final response = await http.post(
      Uri.parse('$baseUrl/mqtt/session'),
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'Authorization': 'Bearer $_jwtToken',
      },
    );

    if (response.statusCode == 200) {
      return jsonDecode(response.body);
    }
    throw Exception('Failed to acquire MQTT session: ${response.body}');
  }

  // 3. Query Historical Points for Charts
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> getHistoricalData(int channelId, {String resolution = 'auto'}) async {
    final response = await http.get(
      Uri.parse('$baseUrl/channels/$channelId/data?resolution=$resolution'),
      headers: {'Authorization': 'Bearer $_jwtToken'},
    );

    if (response.statusCode == 200) {
      return jsonDecode(response.body);
    }
    throw Exception('Failed to load history');
  }
}

docs.title: 3. Real-Time MQTT Client (iot_mqtt_service.dart)
docs.text:
import 'dart:convert';
import 'package:mqtt_client/mqtt_client.dart';
import 'package:mqtt_client/mqtt_server_client.dart'; // Mobile (TCP TLS)
// For Flutter Web, use: import 'package:mqtt_client/mqtt_browser_client.dart';

class IotMqttService {
  final String brokerHost;
  final int port;
  final String username;
  final String password;
  MqttServerClient? _client;

  IotMqttService({
    required this.brokerHost,
    this.port = 8883,
    required this.username,
    required this.password,
  });

  Future<void> connect(int channelId, Function(Map<String, dynamic>) onDataReceived) async {
    _client = MqttServerClient.withPort(brokerHost, 'flutter_${username}', port);
    _client!.secure = true;
    _client!.logging(on: false);
    _client!.keepAlivePeriod = 30;

    final connMessage = MqttConnectMessage()
        .authenticateAs(username, password)
        .withClientIdentifier('flutter_${username}')
        .startClean()
        .withWillQos(MqttQos.atLeastOnce);
    _client!.connectionMessage = connMessage;

    try {
      print('Connecting to MQTT broker at $brokerHost:$port...');
      await _client!.connect();
      print('Connected to MQTT!');

      final topic = 'channels/$channelId/data';
      _client!.subscribe(topic, MqttQos.atLeastOnce);

      _client!.updates!.listen((List<MqttReceivedMessage<MqttMessage>> messages) {
        final recMess = messages[0].payload as MqttPublishMessage;
        final payload = MqttPublishPayload.bytesToStringAsString(recMess.payload.message);

        try {
          final decoded = jsonDecode(payload);
          if (decoded is Map<String, dynamic>) {
            onDataReceived(decoded);
          } else if (decoded is List) {
            for (var item in decoded) {
              if (item is Map<String, dynamic>) {
                onDataReceived(item);
              }
            }
          }
        } catch (e) {
          print('Error decoding MQTT packet: $e');
        }
      });
    } catch (e) {
      print('MQTT connection failed: $e');
      _client?.disconnect();
    }
  }

  void disconnect() {
    _client?.disconnect();
  }
}

docs.title: Live MQTT Streaming & Real-Time Updates
docs.text: A central feature of ThingLarp is immediate, real-time telemetry streaming directly to client dashboards over MQTT, eliminating polling overhead and latency.

docs.title: The Streaming Workflow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor User as User Dashboard
    participant API as FastAPI Gateway
    participant Broker as Mosquitto Broker
    participant Device as Sensor Hardware

    User->>API: POST /mqtt/session (Bearer JWT)
    API-->>User: Ephemeral Credentials (s_xxxx / pass, 24h)
    User->>Broker: CONNECT (Username: s_xxxx, Password: pass)
    Broker-->>User: CONNACK (Authenticated)
    User->>Broker: SUBSCRIBE channels/42/data
    Broker-->>User: SUBACK (Authorized via mqtt.acl_topics)

    loop Continuous Sensor Telemetry
        Device->>Broker: PUBLISH channels/42/data {"temp": 24.2, "hum": 55.1}
        Broker-->>User: PUBLISH channels/42/data (Immediate dispatch)
        Note over User: Update live metric cards &<br/>append point to active FL Chart
    end

docs.title: Acquiring Ephemeral Frontend Credentials
docs.text:
To preserve security, end-users never connect using their primary account password. The client requests a dedicated, short-lived session token:

POST /mqtt/session
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT_TOKEN>

Response: 

{
  "username": "s_a1b2c3d4e5f6...",
  "password": "generated_secure_password",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-13T12:00:00Z"
}

This username is stored in app.mqtt_sessions and automatically authorized by mqtt.acl_topics() to read and subscribe only to channels owned by the user or marked public.

docs.title: MQTT Client Implementation (MqttService)
docs.text:
In app/lib/services/mqtt_service.dart, the client manages the connection lifecycle:

class MqttService {
  final AppConfig config;
  MqttServerClient? _client;
  final StreamController<TelemetryMessage> _messageStream = StreamController.broadcast();

  Stream<TelemetryMessage> get messages => _messageStream.stream;

  Future<void> connect(String username, String password) async {
    _client = MqttServerClient(config.mqttHost, 'tl_app_${DateTime.now().millisecondsSinceEpoch}')
      ..port = config.mqttPort
      ..keepAlivePeriod = 30
      ..autoReconnect = true;

    final connMessage = MqttConnectMessage()
        .authenticateAs(username, password)
        .withWillTopic('clients/disconnect')
        .startClean();
    _client!.connectionMessage = connMessage;

    await _client!.connect();

    _client!.updates?.listen((List<MqttReceivedMessage<MqttMessage>> c) {
      final recMess = c[0].payload as MqttPublishMessage;
      final pt = MqttPublishPayload.bytesToStringAsString(recMess.payload.message);
      final json = jsonDecode(pt);

      _messageStream.add(TelemetryMessage(
        time: DateTime.now(),
        channelId: parseChannelId(c[0].topic),
        payload: json,
      ));
    });
  }

  void subscribeToChannel(int channelId) {
    _client?.subscribe('channels/$channelId/data', MqttQos.atMostOnce);
  }
}

docs.title: Auto-Reconnection & State Resilience
docs.text:
1. Network Dropouts: If the device loses internet access, the client activates an exponential backoff reconnection strategy.
  2. Session Expiry (24 hours): When an ephemeral token expires, the client transparently calls POST /mqtt/session to obtain a fresh session credential and reconnects seamlessly.

docs.title: Developer API Tutorial & Integration Guide
docs.text: Welcome to the ThingLarp Developer Tutorial! This guide is designed to be beginner-friendly while providing production-ready code examples for streaming and querying telemetry using the ThingLarp REST API and MQTT broker.

docs.title: 🌟 Why the ThingLarp API is Different
docs.text:
If you have used legacy IoT platforms like ThingSpeak, you may be familiar with strict limits: - ❌ Throttled to 1 update every 15–60 seconds. - ❌ Restricted to 8 numeric fields (field1 through field8). - ❌ Rigid predefined database schemas.

ThingLarp removes these restrictions entirely: - ⚡ Zero Artificial Rate Limits: Stream at 10Hz, 50Hz, or 100Hz continuously. - 📈 Unlimited Dynamic Fields: Send arbitrary JSON payloads (e.g., {"temperature": 24.5, "pressure_kpa": 101.3, "status": "nominal"}). - 🔄 Dual-Ingress Parity: Any data sent via HTTP REST is forwarded immediately to live MQTT subscribers, and vice-versa.

docs.title: 🔑 Core Concepts & Authentication
docs.text:
Before making requests, understand the three essential identifiers:

Identifier Where to Find It What It's Used For Channel ID Top of Channel screen (e.g. 42) Identifies your telemetry stream container. API Key (X-API-Key) Channel Detail -> API Keys Tab Used for authenticating HTTP REST requests (write or read scope). Device Credentials Channel Detail -> Devices Tab Dedicated username (d_...) and password for hardware connecting via MQTT.

docs.title: 🛠️ In-App Tutorial & Code Generator
docs.text:
Did you know the ThingLarp Flutter App includes a built-in interactive code generator?

  • From the Channels screen: Click the graduation cap icon (🎓) in the top AppBar.
  • From a specific Channel: Click the API Guide icon (🎓) or tap the HTTP REST API Tutorials banner inside the API Keys tab.
  • Pre-Filled Code: All code snippets automatically populate with your active Channel ID, API Base URL, and API Key!
  • Live Test Console: Includes an in-app ping simulator to send test JSON packets directly to your channel without leaving the UI.

docs.title: 🚀 Tutorial 1: Sending Telemetry (HTTP POST)
docs.text: To ingest telemetry, send an HTTP POST request to /channels/{channel_id}/data.

docs.title: Request Specifications
docs.text:
• URL: https://api.iimarky123.io.vn/channels/{channel_id}/data
  • Method: POST
  • Headers:
  • Content-Type: application/json
  • X-API-Key: tl_write_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
  • Body: Any valid JSON object with key-value pairs.

docs.title: Interactive Code Examples
Expected Response
docs.text:
On success, the API returns HTTP 202 Accepted: 

{
  "status": "published",
  "channel_id": 1
}

docs.title: 1. Fetch Latest Snapshot
docs.text:
Retrieve the single most recent JSON packet received by the channel:

curl -X GET "https://api.iimarky123.io.vn/channels/1/latest" \
  -H "X-API-Key: tl_read_YOUR_KEY_HERE"

Response: 

{
  "channel_id": 1,
  "time": "2026-11-12T08:35:10.123456Z",
  "payload": {
    "temperature": 24.5,
    "humidity": 58.2,
    "status": "online"
  }
}

docs.title: 2. Query Historical Time-Series
docs.text:
Query downsampled historical charts:

curl -X GET "https://api.iimarky123.io.vn/channels/1/data?resolution=auto&fields=temperature,humidity" \
  -H "X-API-Key: tl_read_YOUR_KEY_HERE"

docs.title: Query Parameters:
docs.text:
• resolution:
  • auto (Default): Automatically chooses the best resolution based on your time window.
  • raw: Returns individual microsecond sensor readings (best for windows < 6 hours).
  • 1m: Returns 1-minute pre-computed rollup aggregates (best for windows up to 14 days).
  • 1h: Returns 1-hour pre-computed rollup aggregates (best for multi-month queries).
  • fields: Optional comma-separated list of field keys to filter (e.g. temperature,battery_v).
  • start / end: Optional ISO 8601 timestamps (defaults to the last 24 hours).

docs.title: 3. Downloading / Exporting Telemetry (CSV & JSON)
docs.text:
ThingLarp provides a streaming export endpoint to download telemetry for offline analysis in Excel, pandas, or backup systems:

Export as CSV SpreadsheetExport as JSON Array 
curl -X GET "https://api.iimarky123.io.vn/channels/1/export?format=csv&resolution=raw" \
  -H "X-API-Key: tl_read_YOUR_KEY_HERE" \
  -o channel_1_telemetry.csv

curl -X GET "https://api.iimarky123.io.vn/channels/1/export?format=json&resolution=1m" \
  -H "X-API-Key: tl_read_YOUR_KEY_HERE" \
  -o channel_1_telemetry.json

docs.title: 4. Clearing Channel Telemetry Data
docs.text:
To wipe all historical readings and message logs while retaining field definitions:

curl -X DELETE "https://api.iimarky123.io.vn/channels/1/data" \
  -H "X-API-Key: tl_write_YOUR_KEY_HERE"

Response: 

{
  "status": "cleared",
  "channel_id": 1,
  "detail": "All telemetry points and messages have been cleared."
}

docs.title: ⚡ Tutorial 3: Real-Time Telemetry Streaming via MQTT
docs.text: When building embedded microcontroller firmware (ESP32, STM32, Raspberry Pi Pico), MQTT is strongly recommended over HTTP because: 1. Low Overhead: Single persistent TCP TLS socket avoids opening and closing TLS handshakes on every reading. 2. High Throughput: Easily stream at 50Hz–100Hz without CPU or memory spikes. 3. Bi-Directional: Devices can both publish telemetry and listen for remote commands.

docs.title: MQTT Connection Parameters
docs.text:
• Broker Host: mqtt.iimarky123.io.vn
  • MQTTS Port (TLS): 8883
  • Telemetry Topic: channels/{channel_id}/data
  • Username: d_YOUR_DEVICE_USERNAME (generated under Channel -> Devices)
  • Password: YOUR_DEVICE_PASSWORD

docs.title: Publishing via Mosquitto CLI
docs.text:
mosquitto_pub -h "mqtt.iimarky123.io.vn" -p 8883 \
  -u "d_my_sensor_node" \
  -P "my_device_secret_password" \
  -t "channels/1/data" \
  -m '{"temperature": 25.1, "humidity": 59.3}'

docs.title: Subscribing to Live Channel Events
docs.text:
mosquitto_sub -h "mqtt.iimarky123.io.vn" -p 8883 \
  -u "d_my_sensor_node" \
  -P "my_device_secret_password" \
  -t "channels/1/data" -v

docs.title: 📡 Tutorial 4: Downlink Device Remote Control & Actuation
docs.text: ThingLarp supports bidirectional IoT communication. You can dispatch commands from the web/mobile app or HTTP API down to your edge devices (ESP32, Raspberry Pi, relays, motors) in real time.

docs.title: How Downlink Dispatch Works
docs.text:
1. You make an HTTP request to POST /channels/{channel_id}/commands.
  2. The ThingLarp API publishes the payload to MQTT topic channels/{channel_id}/{subtopic} (default: channels/{channel_id}/commands) at QoS 1.
  3. Connected devices subscribed to this topic immediately receive the JSON payload and execute the requested action.

docs.title: Dispatching via cURL
docs.text:
curl -X POST "https://api.iimarky123.io.vn/channels/1/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: tl_write_YOUR_KEY_HERE" \
  -d '{
    "payload": {
      "relay": 1,
      "state": "ON"
    },
    "subtopic": "commands"
  }'

docs.title: Receiving Commands on ESP32 (Arduino C++)
docs.text:
Make sure the provisioned device scope is set to subscribe or pubsub: 

void callback(char* topic, byte* payload, unsigned int length) {
  StaticJsonDocument<256> doc;
  deserializeJson(doc, payload, length);

  if (doc.containsKey("relay")) {
    int relayNum = doc["relay"];
    const char* state = doc["state"];
    if (strcmp(state, "ON") == 0) {
      digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, HIGH);
    } else {
      digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, LOW);
    }
  }
}

// In setup / reconnect logic:
client.subscribe("channels/1/commands", 1);

docs.title: Receiving Commands in Python
docs.text:
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import json

def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    cmd = json.loads(msg.payload.decode())
    print(f"Received command on {msg.topic}: {cmd}")
    if cmd.get("relay") == 1 and cmd.get("state") == "ON":
        print("Actuator: Turning Relay ON!")

client = mqtt.Client()
client.tls_set()
client.username_pw_set("d_esp32_node", "YOUR_DEVICE_PASSWORD")
client.on_message = on_message
client.connect("mqtt.iimarky123.io.vn", 8883)
client.subscribe("channels/1/commands", qos=1)
client.loop_forever()

docs.title: 📥 Tutorial 5: Data Migration & CSV Import Tool
docs.text: Have existing historical telemetry from ThingSpeak or another platform? ThingLarp provides an automated CSV import engine that parses historical timestamps and registers all discovered fields in TimescaleDB.

docs.title: Supported CSV Formats
docs.text:
1. ThingSpeak Export Format:

2026-11-12T00:00:00Z,1,24.5,60.2
2026-11-12T01:00:00Z,2,25.1,58.9

2026-11-12 12:05:00,25.1,58.9,460

  -H "Content-Type: text/csv" \
  -H "X-API-Key: tl_write_YOUR_KEY_HERE" \

docs.text:
1. Open the Channel Dashboard.
  2. Tap the top-right menu (⋮) and select Import Data (CSV).
  3. Click Load Sample ThingSpeak CSV to test or paste your exported CSV text directly.
  4. Tap Start Import — your charts and snapshot metrics will update immediately!

docs.title: ❓ HTTP Status Codes & Troubleshooting
docs.text: HTTP Code Meaning Common Cause & Solution 202 Accepted Success Telemetry published to MQTT broker and ingested into TimescaleDB. 200 OK Success Historical or latest data returned successfully. 400 Bad Request Invalid JSON The payload body is not valid JSON. Ensure quotes around keys ({"temp": 25}). 401 Unauthorized Missing Credentials No X-API-Key or Authorization header provided. 403 Forbidden Scope Mismatch Using a read API key for a POST write operation. Generate a write key. 404 Not Found Unknown Channel The Channel ID does not exist or has been deleted. 503 Unavailable Broker Offline The API could not reach Mosquitto. Check broker container status.

docs.title: Configuring the Environment (.env)
docs.text: The .env file at the root of the project is the single source of truth for the entire ThingLarp platform. It supplies configuration parameters, database credentials, domain names, and cryptographic keys to Docker Compose, which automatically distributes them across all microservices.

docs.title: 1. Initial Setup
docs.text:
To begin, copy the provided template to create your active .env file:

cp .env.example .env

Ensure the file permissions restrict read access to authorized system users:

chmod 600 .env

docs.title: Section 1: Domain & TLS Configuration
docs.text:
These variables configure Traefik v3 for routing and automated SSL/TLS certificate issuance via Let's Encrypt:

# Domain & TLS Configuration
DOMAIN=example.com
API_DOMAIN=api.example.com
MQTT_DOMAIN=mqtt.example.com
ACME_EMAIL=admin@example.com
  • DOMAIN: The base apex domain of your organization or project.
  • API_DOMAIN: Subdomain routed to the FastAPI Gateway (HTTPS on port 443).
  • MQTT_DOMAIN: Subdomain routed to the Mosquitto broker with TLS termination (MQTTS on port 8883).
  • ACME_EMAIL: The email address submitted to Let's Encrypt for registration and expiration warnings.

[!IMPORTANT] DNS Prerequisite for Production: Before starting Traefik, ensure you have configured A or CNAME records with your DNS registrar pointing api.example.com and mqtt.example.com to your public server IP. Let's Encrypt requires successful HTTP-01 challenge resolution on port 80.

For Local Development / LAN: You can leave these as defaults or point them to localhost. Local traffic accesses the API on http://localhost:8000 and MQTT on port 1883 directly without TLS.

docs.title: Section 2: PostgreSQL Superuser & Database
docs.text:
These settings configure the core PostgreSQL 16 container running TimescaleDB:

# PostgreSQL Root & App Database
POSTGRES_DB=iot
POSTGRES_USER=postgres
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres_supersecret_change_me
  • POSTGRES_DB: The database name initialized inside the cluster (defaults to iot).
  • POSTGRES_USER: The PostgreSQL administrative superuser account (defaults to postgres).
  • POSTGRES_PASSWORD: The master password for the administrative user. Replace with a random password.

docs.title: Section 3: Service Database Passwords
docs.text:
ThingLarp enforces strict least-privilege security. Each service connects to PostgreSQL using a dedicated database role with restricted table permissions:

# Service Database Passwords (automatically synced to db/init/03_roles.sh)
PG_MQTT_AUTH_PASSWORD=iot_mqtt_auth_secret
PG_BRIDGE_PASSWORD=iot_bridge_secret
PG_API_PASSWORD=iot_api_secret
  • PG_MQTT_AUTH_PASSWORD: Password for the iot_mqtt_auth user, consumed by the mosquitto-go-auth plugin to query credentials and ACLs.
  • PG_BRIDGE_PASSWORD: Password for the iot_bridge user, used by the Python Ingestion Bridge to bulk COPY telemetry into TimescaleDB.
  • PG_API_PASSWORD: Password for the iot_api user, used by the FastAPI Gateway for user registration, channel management, and telemetry queries.

[!NOTE] Fully Automated Synchronization: Database roles and passwords are automatically generated on first cluster startup via db/init/03_roles.sh. You no longer need to edit static SQL scripts.

docs.title: Section 4: Internal Service MQTT Credentials
docs.text:
The Python Bridge and FastAPI Gateway connect to the Mosquitto broker as dedicated internal service clients:

# Internal Service MQTT Credentials
BRIDGE_MQTT_USER=svc_bridge
BRIDGE_MQTT_PASSWORD=bridge_mqtt_secret
API_MQTT_USER=svc_api
API_MQTT_PASSWORD=api_mqtt_secret
  • BRIDGE_MQTT_USER / BRIDGE_MQTT_PASSWORD: Credentials used by the Python Bridge to subscribe to $share/ingest/channels/+/data.
  • API_MQTT_USER / API_MQTT_PASSWORD: Credentials used by FastAPI to forward HTTP data writes (POST /channels/{id}/data) directly into the broker.

docs.title: How Mosquitto Validates Service Credentials
docs.text:
The Mosquitto mosquitto-go-auth plugin validates MQTT passwords against Bcrypt hashes in PostgreSQL.

During cluster initialization, db/init/03_roles.sh uses PostgreSQL's native pgcrypto extension (crypt(..., gen_salt('bf', 10))) to auto-compute Bcrypt hashes directly from BRIDGE_MQTT_PASSWORD and API_MQTT_PASSWORD. You do not need to generate hashes manually!

Similarly, Mosquitto's Go-Auth plugin dynamically receives POSTGRES_DB and PG_MQTT_AUTH_PASSWORD from .env on container startup via mosquitto/docker-entrypoint.sh and mosquitto/mosquitto.conf.template.

docs.title: Section 5: Security & JWT Token Settings
docs.text:
These settings configure JSON Web Token issuance for user authentication in the API Gateway and Flutter app:

# Security
JWT_SECRET=super_secret_random_jwt_key_32_chars_min
JWT_ALGORITHM=HS256
ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES=15
REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRE_DAYS=30
  • JWT_SECRET: Cryptographic secret key used to sign and verify user JWTs. Must be at least 32 characters long.
  • JWT_ALGORITHM: Cryptographic signing algorithm (defaults to HS256).
  • ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES: Lifespan of short-lived access tokens (default: 15 minutes).
  • REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRE_DAYS: Lifespan of persistent refresh tokens (default: 30 days).

docs.title: 3. Generating Secure Production Secrets
docs.text:
For production environments, you can generate cryptographically secure random values using openssl or python:

Generate JWT Secret (64 hex characters)Generate Strong Passwords 
openssl rand -hex 32

openssl rand -base64 24

docs.title: 4. Applying Changes to Running Containers
docs.text:
When you modify .env, restart the Docker Compose stack to apply the new environment variables:

# Restart services to pick up new environment variables
docker compose up -d

# If database passwords or service credentials were changed from scratch:
docker compose down -v
docker compose up -d --build

[!CAUTION] Running docker compose down -v deletes PostgreSQL storage volumes. Only use -v during initial setup or when you intend to wipe the database.

docs.title: Getting Started Guide
docs.text: This step-by-step guide walks you through setting up and running the entire ThingLarp IoT platform locally or on a cloud virtual machine.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure you have the following installed on your host machine:

  • Docker Engine (v24.0 or newer) and Docker Compose v2
  • Git
  • Python 3.11+ (for test scripts and CLI tools)
  • Flutter SDK 3.24+ (if building or running the Flutter dashboard)

docs.title: 1. Clone the Repository & Configure Environment
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/iimarky1234/thinglarp.git
cd thinglarp

Copy the example environment configuration:

cp .env.example .env

Review the .env settings: - In local development, the default database passwords and service secrets can be used as-is. - For production, replace DOMAIN, ACME_EMAIL, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, and JWT_SECRET with strong, unique secrets.

[!TIP] For a complete parameter breakdown, secret generation commands, and production security checklists, see the dedicated Environment Configuration (.env) Guide.

docs.title: 2. Start the Backend Infrastructure
docs.text:
Start all Docker containers using Docker Compose:

docker compose up -d --build

Verify that all services are healthy and running:

docker compose ps

You should see 5 running containers:

Container Name Service Status Exposed Ports iot_traefik Traefik v3 Up 80, 443, 8883 (Sole Public Ingress), 127.0.0.1:8080 iot_mosquitto Mosquitto Up 1883, 9001 (internal Docker networks only) iot_api FastAPI Gateway Up 8000 (internal Docker networks only) iot_bridge Python Bridge Up internal iot_timescaledb TimescaleDB Up (healthy) 5432 (isolated internal network)

docs.title: 3. Verify System Health
docs.text:
Run an HTTP health check through Traefik:

# Direct via Traefik (using domain host header)
curl -H "Host: ${API_DOMAIN:-api.example.com}" http://localhost/health

Expected response: 

{"status":"ok","database":"connected","mqtt_publisher":"connected"}

docs.title: 4. Run the End-to-End Simulation
docs.text:
Execute the automated end-to-end verification script to confirm database creation, MQTT broker authentication, Python ingestion, TimescaleDB rollups, and API key ingestion:

python scripts/e2e_simulation.py

All 14 simulation steps will execute and print green checkmarks (✅).

docs.title: 5. Launch the Flutter Application
docs.text:
Navigate to the app/ folder and launch the native desktop application:

cd app/
flutter run -d linux

Log in with the pre-provisioned administrator credentials: - Username: admin - Password: admin123456

(When logged in as an administrator, click the shield / admin icon in the top AppBar to access the Admin User Management console to manage accounts, reset passwords, or review platform statistics).

docs.text:
#include <WiFi.h>
#include <PubSubClient.h>
#include <ArduinoJson.h>

const char* ssid = "YOUR_WIFI_SSID";
const char* password = "YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD";

const char* mqtt_server = "192.168.1.100"; // Or domain name
const int mqtt_port = 1883;

// Device Credentials
const char* mqtt_user = "d_e92ab04d7c";
const char* mqtt_pass = "super_secret_generated_password";
const char* topic = "channels/1/data";

WiFiClient espClient;
PubSubClient client(espClient);

void setup_wifi() {
  delay(10);
  WiFi.begin(ssid, password);
  while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) {
    delay(500);
  }
}

void reconnect() {
  while (!client.connected()) {
    if (client.connect("ESP32_Weather_Node", mqtt_user, mqtt_pass)) {
      Serial.println("Connected to ThingLarp Broker!");
    } else {
      delay(2000);
    }
  }
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  setup_wifi();
  client.setServer(mqtt_server, mqtt_port);
}

void loop() {
  if (!client.connected()) {
    reconnect();
  }
  client.loop();

  // Create Dynamic JSON Payload
  StaticJsonDocument<200> doc;
  doc["temperature"] = 24.5 + random(-10, 10) / 10.0;
  doc["humidity"] = 55.0 + random(-20, 20) / 10.0;
  doc["voltage"] = 3.71;
  doc["rssi"] = WiFi.RSSI();

  char buffer[256];
  serializeJson(doc, buffer);

  // Publish to ThingLarp
  client.publish(topic, buffer);
  Serial.print("Published: ");
  Serial.println(buffer);

  delay(2000); // Publish every 2 seconds
}

docs.title: Simulation & Verification Scripts
docs.text: ThingLarp includes automated Python simulation scripts in the scripts/ directory to facilitate integration testing, stress testing, and dashboard demonstration without physical hardware.

docs.title: 1. End-to-End Test Suite (scripts/e2e_simulation.py)
docs.text:
The end-to-end simulation script executes a full lifecycle verification across all platform microservices:

python scripts/e2e_simulation.py

docs.title: Steps Executed
docs.text:
1. User Registration & Login: Generates a new unique user and retrieves a JWT access token.
  2. Channel Creation: Provisions a new private channel via REST.
  3. Hardware Device Provisioning: Creates an ESP32 hardware credential with Bcrypt password.
  4. MQTT Frontend Session: Requests a short-lived ephemeral session token for a client app.
  5. Real-Time MQTT Pub/Sub: Connects the app subscriber and ESP32 publisher over MQTT, verifying real-time packet delivery.
  6. Multi-Tenant Security Enforcement: Verifies that attempting to publish to unauthorized channels is immediately rejected by Mosquitto's ACL engine.
  7. Dynamic Field Auto-Discovery: Publishes 10 unconfigured dynamic fields (voltage, current, power, rpm, vibration_x, etc.) and asserts they are registered in app.channel_fields.
  8. TimescaleDB Continuous Aggregates: Confirms 1-minute and 1-hour continuous aggregate rollups contain valid materialized buckets.
  9. HTTP Ingestion: Generates a Write API Key and sends data via POST /channels/{id}/data, confirming both broker fan-out and database persistence.

docs.title: 2. Live Telemetry Stream Generator (scripts/stream_generator.py)
docs.text: The stream generator creates fluctuating waveforms (sine/cosine oscillations with simulated sensor noise) to animate graphs in the Flutter dashboard in real time.

  --device d_xxxxxxxx your_device_password \

docs.title: Production Security Recommendations
docs.text:
1. Rotate Secrets: Never use default passwords or default JWT_SECRET in production.
  2. Synchronize Role Hashes: If you change BRIDGE_MQTT_PASSWORD or API_MQTT_PASSWORD, generate new Bcrypt hashes (cost 10) and update db/init/03_roles.sql prior to first database initialization.
  3. Restrict Docker Socket: Ensure /var/run/docker.sock mounted into Traefik is protected and inaccessible from untrusted networks.

docs.title: MQTT Topics & Authorization Matrix
docs.text: This document outlines the MQTT topic structure and topic-level access control rules enforced by mosquitto-go-auth and mqtt.acl_topics().

docs.title: Topic Naming Conventions
docs.text:
All MQTT topics follow strict hierarchical namespaces:

channels/
└── {channel_id}/
    ├── data       # High-frequency JSON sensor telemetry
    ├── commands   # Downlink actuator commands (relays, triggers, configs)
    └── status     # Last Will and Testament (LWT) & online status

docs.title: Authorization Permission Matrix
docs.text:
mosquitto-go-auth passes an integer access flag into PostgreSQL: - 1 = Read - 2 = Write - 4 = Subscribe

Topic Pattern Client Identity Allowed Operations Condition / Evaluation Logic channels/{id}/data Hardware Device (d_*) Write (2) Device is active (is_active = true) and scope is publish or pubsub. channels/{id}/data Hardware Device (d_*) Sub (4), Read (1) Device is active and scope is subscribe or pubsub. channels/{id}/commands Hardware Device (d_*) Sub (4), Read (1) Device is active and scope is subscribe or pubsub. Receives downlink control payloads. channels/{id}/status Hardware Device (d_*) Write (2) Device is active and scope is publish or pubsub. Used for LWT messages. channels/{id}/data User Frontend Session (s_*) Sub (4), Read (1) Channel {id} is owned by user or has is_public = true. channels/{id}/status User Frontend Session (s_*) Sub (4), Read (1) Same as data channel. channels/{id}/commands API Service Account (svc_api) Write (2) Dispatches HTTP command requests to MQTT. $share/ingest/channels/+/data Ingestion Bridge (svc_bridge) Sub (4) Dedicated ingestion bridge shared consumer group. # (All Topics) Service Accounts (svc_bridge, svc_api) Superuser System services bypass topic checks.

docs.title: Example Ingestion Payloads
docs.text:
Payloads published to channels/{id}/data must be valid JSON objects. Numeric values are automatically cataloged as discrete time-series points:

{
  "temp_c": 22.45,
  "humidity_rh": 58.1,
  "lux": 340.0,
  "vibration": 0.003,
  "metadata": {
    "node_fw": "v1.4.2",
    "boot_count": 12
  }
}
  • temp_c, humidity_rh, lux, and vibration are parsed into individual time-series entries in telemetry.points.
  • The entire JSON payload (including metadata) is preserved verbatim in telemetry.messages.

docs.title: REST & Authentication API Gateway
docs.text: The API Gateway (api/) is a high-performance FastAPI service responsible for user authentication, channel management, device provisioning, API key issuance, and telemetry queries.

docs.title: Technical Highlights
docs.text:
• Framework: FastAPI with Python 3.12+ and uvicorn.
  • Database Driver: asyncpg with a pooled connection manager (api/database.py).
  • Security:
  • User Passwords: Argon2id (via pwdlib[argon2]).
  • Hardware / Session Credentials: Bcrypt (cost 10) for compatibility with mosquitto-go-auth.
  • Tokens: Signed JWTs (HS256) with 15-minute access expiration and 30-day refresh tokens.
  • HTTP API Keys: Cryptographic SHA-256 hash storage.
  • Direct MQTT Forwarding: An internal persistent MQTT client (api/mqtt_client.py) forwards HTTP data writes directly into the broker so live WebSocket and MQTT subscribers receive immediate events.

docs.title: Router Modules
docs.text: Router Path Prefix Description auth /auth User registration, login (JWT generation), token refresh, and user profile. channels /channels Channel CRUD, field listings, and public/private channel access control. devices /channels/{id}/devices Hardware device provisioning, credentials rotation, and listing. keys /channels/{id}/keys Write / Read API key generation and revocation. mqtt /mqtt Short-lived (24h) MQTT session generation for frontend clients (POST /mqtt/session). data /channels/{id}/data Telemetry query with auto-downsampling and HTTP ingestion (POST). admin /admin Administrative user management, privilege modification, and platform metrics (is_admin = true).

docs.title: Dynamic Telemetry Query & Auto-Downsampling
docs.text:
When querying telemetry (GET /channels/{id}/data), the API dynamically selects the optimal storage representation based on the requested time window:

# api/routers/data.py
if resolution == "auto":
    delta = end_time - start_time
    if delta > timedelta(days=14):
        target_resolution = "1h" # Query telemetry.points_1h
    elif delta > timedelta(hours=6):
        target_resolution = "1m" # Query telemetry.points_1m
    else:
        target_resolution = "raw" # Query telemetry.points

docs.title: Response Schema
docs.text:
{
  "channel_id": 42,
  "start": "2026-11-12T00:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-12T12:00:00Z",
  "resolution": "1m",
  "fields": {
    "1": "temperature",
    "2": "humidity"
  },
  "points": [
    {
      "time": "2026-11-12T00:00:00Z",
      "field": "temperature",

docs.title: HTTP Ingestion Endpoint (Dual-Ingress)
docs.text:
Devices or external webhook services can publish via simple HTTP:

POST /channels/42/data
Host: api.example.com
X-API-Key: tl_write_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "temperature": 25.4,
  "humidity": 60.2,
  "status": "normal"
}
  1. The API validates the X-API-Key against app.api_keys where scope = 'write'.
  2. It publishes the payload directly to the internal MQTT broker on topic channels/42/data.
  3. Mosquitto fans the message out to the Python Ingestion Bridge (for DB persistence) and all active Flutter/Web subscribers simultaneously.

docs.title: Ingestion Bridge Service
docs.text: The Ingestion Bridge (bridge/) is a dedicated Python microservice designed for low-latency, high-throughput message processing between Eclipse Mosquitto and TimescaleDB.

docs.title: Core Responsibilities
docs.text:
1. Shared MQTT Consumer: Subscribes to $share/ingest/channels/+/data to distribute load across worker instances without duplicate ingestion.
  2. Fast JSON Parsing: Uses orjson (written in Rust) to parse JSON payloads up to 10x faster than standard Python json.
  3. Dynamic Field Auto-Discovery: Extracts arbitrary numeric fields without requiring the user to configure columns in advance.
  4. RAM Field ID Caching: Resolves field names to integer field_ids in RAM to prevent database lookups on every packet.
  5. PostgreSQL Binary COPY Batching: Accumulates parsed points in memory and flushes them into TimescaleDB using binary COPY protocol.

docs.title: Architecture of the Bridge
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    MQTT["MQTT Broker<br><code>$share/ingest/channels/+/data</code>"] -->|"aiomqtt"| INGEST["Ingestion Consumer"]
    INGEST -->|"Raw Bytes"| PARSER["orjson Parser"]

    subgraph RAM_STATE["In-Memory State"]
        PARSER -->|"Numeric Fields"| CACHE["FieldCache (RAM)"]
        CACHE -->|"field_id + value"| BATCHER["TelemetryBatcher (RAM)"]
    end

    CACHE <-->|"Auto-register new fields"| TS_FIELDS["app.channel_fields"]
    BATCHER ==>|"COPY Protocol Flush (2000 pts or 500ms)"| TS_POINTS["telemetry.points"]
    BATCHER ==>|"COPY Protocol Flush (raw JSON)"| TS_MSGS["telemetry.messages"]

docs.title: In-Memory Caching & Guardrails
docs.text:
When a device publishes a new field name (e.g. "battery_pct"):

  1. FieldCache checks its internal dictionary (channel_id, field_name) -> field_id.
  2. If absent:
  3. Verifies the channel has not exceeded max_fields_per_channel (default: 500 fields) to protect against malicious key flooding.
  4. Inserts the new field into app.channel_fields with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.
  5. Caches the resulting field_id.
class FieldCache:
    def __init__(self, pool, max_fields_per_channel=500):
        self._cache = {} # (channel_id, name) -> field_id
        self._counts = {} # channel_id -> count
        self._max_fields = max_fields_per_channel

docs.title: PostgreSQL Binary COPY Micro-Batching
docs.text:
Individual INSERT statements incur substantial network round-trip overhead. The Bridge uses asyncpg's copy_records_to_table:

class TelemetryBatcher:
    def __init__(self, pool, max_batch_size=2000, max_interval=0.5):
        self._points = []
        self._messages = []
        self._max_batch_size = max_batch_size
        self._max_interval = max_interval

    async def flush(self):
        if not self._points and not self._messages:
            return

        async with self._pool.acquire() as conn:
            async with conn.transaction():
                if self._points:
                    await conn.copy_records_to_table(
                        "points",
                        records=self._points,
                        columns=["time", "channel_id", "field_id", "value"],
                        schema_name="telemetry",
                    )
                if self._messages:
                    await conn.copy_records_to_table(
                        "messages",
                        records=self._messages,
                        columns=["time", "channel_id", "device_id", "payload"],
                        schema_name="telemetry",
                    )

docs.title: Flush Trigger Triggers
docs.text: The buffer flushes to PostgreSQL whenever: - The buffer reaches 2,000 points, OR - 0.5 seconds elapses since the last write, whichever occurs first.

docs.title: MQTT Broker Service (Mosquitto)
docs.text: ThingLarp uses Eclipse Mosquitto augmented with the mosquitto-go-auth plugin to provide high-concurrency, strictly authenticated MQTT messaging.

docs.title: Network Listeners & Protocols
docs.text:
The broker exposes three network listeners:

Port Protocol Listener Role Target Clients 1883 Plain TCP Internal Docker network & Local testing Bridge service, internal API forwarder, local devices 8883 TCP + TLS (via Traefik) Secure public MQTTS Production IoT devices, Flutter desktop & mobile apps 9001 WebSockets / WSS (via Traefik) Browser WebSockets Flutter Web applications

docs.title: Dynamic Authentication (mosquitto-go-auth)
docs.text: Rather than maintaining static password files (passwd) or static ACL text files, mosquitto-go-auth queries PostgreSQL in real time.

docs.title: Dynamic Configuration (mosquitto.conf.template)
docs.text:
Mosquitto generates its active configuration at container startup using mosquitto/docker-entrypoint.sh from mosquitto/mosquitto.conf.template, interpolating ${POSTGRES_DB} and ${PG_MQTT_AUTH_PASSWORD} dynamically from .env:

auth_plugin /usr/lib/mosquitto/go-auth.so
auth_opt_backends postgres

# Dynamic PostgreSQL Connection (injected from .env)
auth_opt_pg_host timescaledb
auth_opt_pg_port 5432
auth_opt_pg_dbname ${POSTGRES_DB}
auth_opt_pg_user iot_mqtt_auth
auth_opt_pg_password ${PG_MQTT_AUTH_PASSWORD}

# Password validation uses Bcrypt
auth_opt_hasher bcrypt

# Authentication SQL Query
auth_opt_pg_userquery SELECT password_hash FROM mqtt.users_view WHERE username = $1 LIMIT 1

# Superuser Query (for internal microservices: svc_bridge, svc_api)
auth_opt_pg_superquery SELECT CASE WHEN username IN ('svc_bridge', 'svc_api') THEN true ELSE false END FROM mqtt.users_view WHERE username = $1

# ACL Authorization Query
# $1: Username
# $2: Access flag (1 = Read, 2 = Write, 4 = Subscribe)
auth_opt_pg_aclquery SELECT topic FROM mqtt.acl_topics($1, $2::int)

docs.title: In-Memory High-Performance Caching
docs.text:
To prevent pounding the database with identical authorization queries during bursts, mosquitto-go-auth enables an in-memory cache:

auth_opt_cache true
auth_opt_cache_type go-cache
auth_opt_auth_cache_seconds 30
auth_opt_acl_cache_seconds 30
auth_opt_auth_jitter_seconds 5
auth_opt_acl_jitter_seconds 5

docs.title: Topic Hierarchy & Permissions
docs.text:
All messages conform to standard topic conventions:

Topic Pattern Permission Flag Who Can Access channels/{id}/data Write (2) Device assigned to channel {id} or svc_api channels/{id}/data Read / Sub (1 / 4) User owning channel {id}, valid session, or if channel is public channels/{id}/status Write (2) Device assigned to channel {id} (LWT message) $share/ingest/channels/+/data Sub (4) svc_bridge (Ingestion Bridge shared subscription) # (All Topics) Superuser svc_bridge (Read-only), svc_api (Write-only)

docs.title: Edge Reverse Proxy (Traefik v3)
docs.text: ThingLarp uses Traefik v3 as its unified ingress and TLS termination point. It sits between public networks and internal Docker containers, managing SSL/TLS certificates automatically via Let's Encrypt.

docs.title: Port Allocation & Routing Rules
docs.text:
Traefik Ingress
├── :80    (HTTP)   -> Redirect to HTTPS & ACME challenge validation
├── :443   (HTTPS)  -> FastAPI Gateway (Host: api.example.com) & WebSockets
├── :8883  (MQTTS)  -> Mosquitto TCP listener (:1883) with TLS termination
└── :8080  (Admin)  -> Traefik Dashboard (Internal / Protected)

docs.title: Static Configuration (traefik/traefik.yml)
docs.text:
entryPoints:
  web:
    address: ":80"
    http:
      redirections:
        entryPoint:
          to: websecure
          scheme: https
          permanent: true

  websecure:
    address: ":443"

  mqtts:
    address: ":8883"

certificatesResolvers:
  letsencrypt:
    acme:
      storage: "/letsencrypt/acme.json"
      httpChallenge:
        entryPoint: "web"

providers:
  docker:
    endpoint: "unix:///var/run/docker.sock"
    exposedByDefault: false
    network: "iot_edge"

[!NOTE] Traefik receives the Let's Encrypt account email dynamically via command flag in docker-compose.yml: command: ["--certificatesresolvers.letsencrypt.acme.email=${ACME_EMAIL}"]

docs.text: Services dynamically register with Traefik using Docker labels in docker-compose.yml:

  - "traefik.docker.network=iot_edge"
  - "traefik.http.routers.mqtt-ws.rule=Host(`${MQTT_DOMAIN}`) && PathPrefix(`/mqtt`)"

  - "traefik.docker.network=iot_edge"
  - "traefik.tcp.routers.mqtt-tls.rule=HostSNI(`${MQTT_DOMAIN}`)"
  - "traefik.tcp.routers.mqtt-tls.entrypoints=mqtts"

docs.title: Complete Isolation (Production Standard)
docs.text: ThingLarp implements complete edge isolation: - Raw backend ports 1883 (Mosquitto), 8000 (FastAPI), and 5432 (TimescaleDB) are never bound to the host. - Traefik is the exclusive ingress point handling :80 (HTTP redirect), :443 (HTTPS & WSS), and :8883 (MQTTS). - The Traefik dashboard (:8080) is strictly bound to 127.0.0.1:8080 or private VPN interfaces (e.g. Tailscale), preventing public exposure.
